title: Where a human still has to review the work
metaTitle: Human in the loop automation, the line
excerpt: Keep a person on anything a customer will see, pay, or be unable to undo. Draw that review into the workflow as a real control.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper. The diagram is the line between what may run and what a person still has to approve.
caption: The flow on the page is where the review line gets drawn. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where does a human still need to review automation?
faqs.answer: Review anything a customer will see, anything that moves money or commits the company to a number, and anything that is painful or impossible to undo. Filing an internal note or sorting a folder can often run on its own. If you cannot point at the moment a person accepts the risky action, the loop is not real.

faqs.question: What should the review screen show?
faqs.answer: Show the output, the source, and the action approve will take. Reject or edit has to be as available as approve. If nobody reviews in time, the default should be the safe one: do not send, charge, or delete.

faqs.question: How large can the review queue be?
faqs.answer: Small enough that a person can actually look. A hundred items in a morning will be rubber-stamped, which adds a false sense that someone checked. Cap the queue, or narrow what requires a person, and write down the one thing the reviewer is accountable for.

markdown:
Human in the loop automation still needs a person wherever a customer will see the result, pay because of it, or be unable to undo it. Draw that line in the workflow before you celebrate the time saved. A review step that exists only as a good intention will be skipped on a busy day, which is the day it was for.

The machine can gather, draft, sort, and flag. The person accepts, edits, or stops the action that crosses the line. If you cannot point at the moment of acceptance, you do not have a loop. You have a launch button with extra steps.

## The three places the line sits

See. Anything a customer, a user, or the public will read or look at. A reply, a product description, a price on a page, a status in a community, a social post. Drafting is fine. Sending or publishing waits.

Pay. Anything that moves money or commits the company to a number. An invoice total, a refund, a discount, a quote. The model can prepare the figures from records. A person checks the records and the total before it is issued. A wrong draft is cheap. A wrong charge is the business.

Undo. Anything that is painful or impossible to reverse. Deleting an account, removing a community member, overwriting the only copy of a file, changing a live DNS record, emailing a list. These can be prepared as a staged action with a named approver. They should not run because a rule was almost sure.

If a step is none of the three, it can often run. Filing an internal note, tagging a record for later, or sorting a folder are reversible and private. Let those run, and spend the human attention on the line.

## Make the review a real control

A review that is "someone glances at the channel" is not a control. Specify who may approve, what they are looking at, and what the approve action does.

The screen should show the output, the source it came from, and the action that will happen. A diff is better than a blob when the change is an edit to existing work. A single approve button that publishes ten unseen changes is how mistakes leave in a batch.

Reject has to be as available as approve. The person needs a way to edit and send, to send back for another draft, or to do the task by hand and turn the automation off for that case. If the only comfortable path is approve, people will approve.

Timeouts need a decision too. If nobody reviews by the end of the day, the default should be the safe one. Do not send. Do not charge. Do not delete. A default of "publish anyway" deletes the loop and keeps the risk.

An example, labeled as an exercise: an automation drafts a shipping delay note from the order and the carrier status. It sits in a queue. The person sees the order number, the carrier line, and the draft. They fix a date and send. If the carrier line is missing, there is no approve button, only a link to the order. The missing source is not a soft warning. It is the loop refusing to pretend.

## What the person is actually for

The person is not a slower version of the model. They are the judgment the automation was told not to have. They notice when the source is stale, when the tone is wrong for this customer, and when the action should not happen even though the fields are filled in.

That only works if the queue is small enough to honor. A hundred items a morning will be rubber-stamped, and rubber-stamping is worse than full automation because it adds a false sense that someone looked. Cap the queue. If the volume is that high, narrow the automation so fewer items need a person, or staff the review honestly.

Rotate the duty if one person will burn out and start clicking through. Write down what they are accountable for, in a sentence. "You are checking that the refund amount matches the order, and that we have not already refunded it." A vague "check the AI" produces vague checking.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) apply to AI web interfaces and ask that the interface be operable and understandable. The review screen is that interface. The approver has to reach the control, read the source, and understand what approve will do. A review designed as a wall of model output fails those conditions, and then the loop fails with it.

## Draw the line where the team can see it

Put the line in the same place as the workflow diagram, not in a principle slide. For each step, mark run, draft, or approve. New automations copy the marks. A step that moves from draft to run requires the owner to say why it is no longer in the three categories.

Review the marks when a customer is affected by a miss. Ask which category the step was in, and whether the control was real. Tighten the control or move the step back to draft. Do not add a paragraph of policy and leave the button as it was.

Keep a short log of what the person changed. Not a surveillance file. A note of the edit: date corrected, amount reduced, tone cut. After twenty reviews the notes show whether the automation is close or whether it is guessing. If the same edit appears every time, fix the draft. If the edits are the judgment itself, stop asking the model to draft that part.

Hanabi's work on automations stays inside this line. A bot can take intake and send an alert. A person still decides what a customer is told when the question leaves the script, and what is allowed to charge or delete.

Showing the source and the limit makes the review faster, and it is how the feature earns trust in the first place. That part is [designing an AI feature people can trust](/blog/ai-features-people-trust). Use it when the draft itself is the thing the person has to believe or edit.
